title: Research
text: The mammalian heart is among the tissues that can regenerate shortly after birth but lose this capacity within the first week of life. My postdoctoral work revealed that successful cardiac regeneration depends on active, developmentally restricted immune programs, rather than on the immature or attenuated immune state traditionally associated with the neonatal period. I first demonstrated that the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint pathway is highly active in the neonatal heart and required for regeneration after myocardial infarction. Disruption of this pathway altered the neonatal γδ T cell behavior, promoting cytotoxic and autoreactive features, excessive inflammation, and fibrotic repair. I subsequently identified these γδ T cells as a population of γδT17 cells that accumulates in the injured heart specifically during the regenerative window and supports regeneration through IL-17A. I further showed that IL-17A acts primarily on macrophages and monocytes to initiate a rapid, self-limited inflammatory response that supports injury resolution.

title: Research
text:
Research funding
T cell-mediated regulation of mouse neonatal heart regeneration. American Heart Association, 2025–2028 (Award No. 25CDA1454364). This project studies how neonatal γδ T cells and IL-17A support heart regeneration and whether IL-17A can improve repair after the regenerative window closes.
The role of monocyte infiltration in cardiac regeneration and repair. American Heart Association, 2022–2024 (Award No. 916883). This project examined whether sustained monocyte recruitment shifts the injured neonatal heart from regeneration toward fibrotic repair.

How does the immune system heal the heart?
Lessons from newborns

title: About
text:
Why do several mammalian tissues regenerate early in life yet lose this capacity soon after birth?
Most explanations for the closure of this regenerative window have focused on maturation of the injured tissue itself: changes in proliferative capacity, metabolism, or extracellular matrix. Yet the immune system is undergoing an equally dramatic transformation during this same period, and its contribution to regenerative decline remains underappreciated.
I am an Ecuadorian immunologist interested in how changes in the immune system across the lifespan shape tissue function, repair, and regeneration. I currently conduct research in the laboratory of Dr. Eric Olson at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, where I study the immune mechanisms that enable the mammalian neonatal heart to regenerate after injury. A major goal of my work is to determine whether immune mechanisms that support neonatal regeneration can be harnessed to improve adult tissue repair.
My research combines mouse genetics, immune profiling, lineage tracing, and single cell genomic approaches, and is currently supported by a Career Development Award from the American Heart Association.
Beyond the laboratory, I am interested in building stronger connections between scientists in the Global South and Global North, giving greater visibility to Latin American research, and encouraging young people to consider science as a possible career.
